paragraphs.text: Again a commemoration of martyrs, again feasts of the devout, again a theme for angels, again a festival of the Church. The commemoration is of those who bore witness, but the honor of the martyrs is the glory of the one to whom they bore witness. The martyrs are honored because they suffered for Christ, but Christ is worshiped because he suffered for all. They, through their suffering, raised themselves from lowliness to the heights; but the Savior came down from the height of divinity to the lowliness of humanity, not departing from his dignity but carrying out the dispensation. For we have heard him say, “I am the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep.” In saying this he both showed his love for humankind and proclaimed his authority. To suffer for the sheep belongs to love for humankind; but to lay down his life of himself belongs to authority. He does not submit to force; he carries out a dispensation. And even if the Apostle says that the Father handed him over for us, he does not present the Son’s suffering as forced, but the Son’s will as concurring with the Father’s. The Son hands himself over, not serving under compulsion, but working together with the Father’s purpose. For it is one thing to assist as a slave does, and another to work together as God does. The Only-begotten is the Father’s co-worker, even if the children of the heretics do not like it, who by their own wickedness divide the indivisible nature, and proclaim the Father as creator, the Son as assistant, and the Holy Spirit as minister. They are not even ashamed before the words of Paul, who called the servants of the proclamation not God’s assistants but God’s co-workers, saying, “We are God’s co-workers.” Is Paul a co-worker, and the Son an assistant? So do not ask what Christ said through Isaiah, but what he said through himself. On his own account he is a shepherd, but on your account a sheep; for these two readings have come together today. Isaiah read to the eunuch concerning him, “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter”; and the Savior says, “I am the good shepherd.” Show me, then, the difference between sheep and shepherd: in what respect he is a sheep, and in what respect a shepherd. For if you do not know the difference between the names, how will you recognize his dignity? Clearly he is a sheep because of the suffering of the dispensation, and a shepherd because of the authority of his love for humankind. Though he is God, he is not ashamed to be called a shepherd. We ought to have known him as God and king; but since, as rational human beings, we did not recognize God, he wants us, even as irrational sheep, to recognize the shepherd. If the Savior, coming into the world, had found you a rational human being, he would of course have appeared to you as God. But since he did not find a human being, but a sheep that had been straying since ancient times and calling on the Master through the prophets, “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant,” he therefore hides his royal dignity and puts forward his shepherd’s care. For this reason, from the very beginning, he arranges for his own body to be laid in a manger, and brings into hardship his mother and Joseph, the servant of the dispensation. I would not call Joseph the Savior’s father, nor Mary’s husband, but a partner and intermediary of the mystery. He was the virgin’s betrothed and not her husband: husband in name, but servant of the dispensation. So he is hard-pressed with Mary in Bethlehem, so that because the lodging was so cramped the infant had to be laid in a manger. But the crowding was God’s doing, so that the lover of humankind would of necessity be laid in that place—laid there, I say, for the sake of the dispensation in the flesh. And why does he arrange this? The manger is the table of irrational animals, and humanity had turned to irrationality (“For man, though in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them”); so he places the heavenly food on the table of the beasts, so that those who are beastlike in soul, coming to the manger as to their own table, might find there no longer beasts’ fodder but the one who says, “I am the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world.” He is a sheep, then, because of the dispensation, but God because of his own glory. So he lays down his life for the sheep, not enduring compulsion, as I said before, but taking on a task. For everything that took place in the old worship finds its summing-up in the Savior: whether prophecy or priesthood or kingship, temple or altar or veil, ark or mercy seat, manna or rod or jar, or anything else—everything refers to him.

From the beginning God permitted the children of the Jews the service of sacrifices, not because he took any delight in sacrifices, but because he wanted to draw them away from paganism. And by this means, steering them toward what he wills, he takes on himself what he does not will. Since the mind of the Jews was not yet able to receive spiritual activity, but was enslaved to the custom of the nations and gaped after altars and sacrifices, God took the idolatrous festivals and refashioned them to the pattern of true religion, tolerating what he did not want. A good father, when he sees his child playing with toys, drags him away from the marketplace but at home lets him do whatever he likes, both preserving his decorum and curbing the shamelessness of his play. In the same way God, wishing to reshape them toward true religion through this visible pageantry of festivals, allowed them to sacrifice, gives them an altar, commands sheep to be sacrificed, and goat and ox, and lets them do everything that delighted them. It was not that it gratified God.

That these things were done by way of accommodation, hear how the one who permitted sacrifices through Moses, and commanded many kinds of sacrifice to be made, overturns through the prophets what had been done by concession, showing that he had allowed it as milk for infants and had not given it as solid food. He says through David: “Hear, my people, and I will speak to you, Israel, and I will testify against you: I am God, your God. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are before me continually. I will not accept bulls from your house, nor goats from your flocks.” And so that no one would think he refuses them out of aversion, he explains the reason: it is because he has no need of them, not because of their being offered. He adds: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.” He shows that he does not shake them off in aversion, but calls them to the better, spiritual sacrifice. So from the beginning he permitted sacrifices, not because he was pleased with them, but to reshape toward true religion those who had started out that way. And yielding to the Jewish inclination, being wise and great, in the very concession of sacrifices he prepared in advance an image of things to come, so that even if the sacrifice was useless in itself, it would prove useful because of the image. Pay close attention, for the thought is subtle. The sacrifices were not pleasing to God, nor done according to his will, but by concession; and as they were being performed he imposed on them a type, in the image of Christ’s future dispensation, so that even if they were not acceptable in themselves, they might at least be acceptable because of the image. Through all of them he sets forth an image of Christ and sketches the things to come. If it is a sheep that is sacrificed, it is an image of the Savior; if an ox, an image of the Lord; if a calf, if a heifer, if anything else that was offered, even a dove or a turtledove—everything referred to the Savior. That is why there was a temple, so that the image of the Lord’s temple might be prepared beforehand; that is why a sheep, that is why a priest, that is why a veil. And so as not to stretch out my discourse item by item, take Paul as the interpreter of what has been said, who does not let you conceive of anything apart from Christ, but takes everything up into Christ. Well then: in writing to the Hebrews, wishing to set out the distinctions of the mysteries—what the table meant, what the altar meant, what the veil meant, what the temple, what the priest—he refers them all, in sum, to Christ, and shows that the whole of life is a tabernacle throughout, but that the first tabernacle is a type of the Old Covenant, while the Holy of Holies is a type of the New Covenant. Pay close attention, I beg you. The temple was one whole, but it was divided into different parts: the holy place and the Holy of Holies. The temple is a type of the Lord’s body; hear the Lord saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Just as in that temple some things were seen by everyone and others by the high priest alone, so too in the Savior’s dispensation the divinity and the working of the divinity, though hidden, was at work openly. You have the image of the temple. Now look for me for the veil in the middle, which separated the holy place from the Holy of Holies, and see what sort of veil it was. Again, the veil is an image of the body. Just as the veil stood between the two parts of the place and shut off the view from outside from the sacred rites within, so the Lord’s body was a veil of the divinity, not allowing mortal eyes to gaze at the sight of the Immortal. These are not my words; hear Paul saying, “Since, brothers, we have a new and living way, which he opened for us through the veil, that is, his flesh, let us draw near.” Pay close attention. He called the flesh a temple, and the veil a type of the flesh. Again, the priest went in through the veil once a year. Paul did not leave this out either, but takes it as a type of the Savior and says, “Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by hands, a copy of the true one, but heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.” You see the high priest; see the type. Again, a sheep was sacrificed, and it was an image of the Savior: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter.” A calf was sacrificed, a bull, and all the rest; and the high priest took some of the blood of the victims on his finger, went into the Holy of Holies, and sprinkled it seven times before the mercy seat. The mercy seat itself was a type of the Savior, and the sprinkled blood was a type of him too, so that both the one worshiped and the gift offered to the one worshiped might be one and the same. The bodies of these animals whose blood was brought into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp, and their ash sanctified people: the remains of the slain animals sanctified those who had been defiled. So look: while alive they did not sanctify, but once reduced to ash and completed as a sacrifice, they brought sanctification to the defiled; and the same animals were both burned outside and offered inside. Hence the Apostle says, “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the Holy of Holies were burned outside the camp.” He has stated the type; now he interprets the truth and says, “Therefore Jesus too, in order to sanctify the people, suffered outside the gate.” And what does he add? “Let us, then, go out to him, bearing his reproach.” You have the type; see the truth. Look again at the blood and the mercy seat. The blood was sprinkled, the mercy seat received it, and the atonement was laid upon it. What is the mercy seat? Hear Paul again, saying in the Letter to the Romans: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through his blood, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a mercy seat through faith in his blood.” The blood is his, and the mercy seat is his. I have said all this because the Savior, God and the only-begotten Son of God, became all these things for our sake, not for his own. But what is carried out for our sake is one thing, and what is worshiped for its own sake according to the divinity is another—one thing and another, not now divided, but joined in the dispensation and distinguished in thought.

So whenever you hear “high priest,” or “shepherd,” or “sheep,” or “temple,” or “veil,” or “mercy seat,” or “blood of sprinkling,” or anything of the kind, recognize in all of them the dispensation carried out for your sake.

But when you see the Only-begotten sharing the throne (for this is what the Church proclaimed and displayed in procession), you are not ashamed of the divine oracles. For Wisdom is hymned in the streets, speaks boldly in the squares, and is proclaimed on the tops of the walls. And when you see God’s wisdom and power proclaimed, consider the surpassing glory, the dignity that is before the ages, invulnerable, unchangeable, unalterable. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Everywhere it is “was,” and nowhere “was not.” If you consider the surpassing glory, you will not stumble at the dispensation of the flesh. What I mean is this: if you hear a heretic saying, “The Father who sent me is greater than I,” tell him there is nothing surprising if he is less than the Father because of the dispensation, since he was made lower even than the angels. You are eager, out of malice, to show that he is less than the Father; but I show that, because of the dispensation, he is less even than the angels. You, wishing to construct a difference of essence between Father and Son, bring forward the saying, “The Father who sent me is greater than I”; but I show that, going by the wording, he is less not only than the Father but also than the angels. For the blessed Paul, bringing forward David’s testimony—“What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels”—interpreted it in the Letter to the Hebrews: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death.”

Why, then, do you toil so hard and labor to show that the Son is less than the Father, when he is less even than the angels—not in dignity, but because of the dispensation? Besides, you have heard, “The Father who sent me is greater than I”; do you not hear this gospel saying, which cried out to everyone today, “I and the Father are one”? And notice the difference. Where he says “one,” he did not say “he who sent me” but “the Father.” Where he wanted to show the union and the identity, he did not say, “I and he who sent me are one,” but “I and the Father.” Between Father and Son there is nothing in between. But where he says “greater,” he adds “he who sent me.” For sending is a work of the dispensation, and being sent is an expression not of divinity but of the dispensation. God neither sends nor is sent in a bodily way. Hear how this is so. One who sends, sends into places where he himself is not present. Show me, then, a place empty of the Father; show me a place bare of the Son; show me a place removed from the Spirit. Then there would be room for your reading, if you took it from the wording that one sent and the other was sent. So “he was sent” indicates not a change of place but a bodily appearance. When Scripture says, “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John,” we do not think that John arrived from heaven. For, someone says, if he was already here, how was he sent? But since he was entrusted with a ministry, Scripture called the ministry a sending. Isaiah, in Jerusalem, in the temple itself, saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and lifted up. Though he was in the city and in the temple, and beheld the vision, and was counted worthy to see God as far as is possible for a human being, he heard God saying, “Whom shall I send to this people?” He was among the people—how then is he sent to the people? Thus sending signifies neither a change of place nor a slave’s service, but a dispensation toward humankind. Otherwise, if you are a slave to the wording, then respect the wording. If he was sent, how does he say, “And he who sent me is with me”? No one who sends someone goes along with the one he sends; that is not sending but accompanying. “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” Where is the sending? And so that no one would think “The Father who sent me is with me” was said in the sense of activity and help, he says, “The Father who dwells in me,” in keeping with “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” Isaiah too proclaimed this saying beforehand: “Egypt has toiled, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the Sabeans, tall men, will cross over to you and follow you bound in fetters, and they will bow down to you and pray in you; for God is in you, and there is no God besides you.” How is this possible? If another is in him, how is there no other besides him? “For God is in you, and there is no God besides you.” Is this not an interpretation of the Gospel saying, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and “The two of us are one”? For “There is no God besides you” interprets “We are one.” And see the wisdom of the wording, how full of power it is. “We are one” is a two-edged sword that cuts down the heretics: “one” refutes the madness of the Arians, and “we are” refutes the confusion of Sabellius. “For God is in you, and there is no God besides you.” And to show that he is the same God in God, the prophet adds, “For you are God, and we did not know it.” Did you not know that he is God? Did Moses not proclaim it before you? Were you not born twenty-one generations after Moses? From Moses to David are seven generations, and from David to Isaiah twelve generations; and Isaiah lived two generations before Babylon. So then, the one whom the prophets had proclaimed as God twenty-five generations earlier—Moses said, “Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one”; Samuel cried out the same; David too proclaimed the same; and every prophet prophesied the same—how could the prophet Isaiah say, “For you are God, and we did not know it,” unless he is truly hinting at the Savior, who exists but is not recognized? “You are God, and we did not know it” does not accuse his own ignorance; he is speaking in the person of the people. The teaching “You are God, and we did not know it” agrees with the one who says, “Lord, your arm is lifted high, and they did not know it.” And as for his saying, “For you are God, and they did not know it, the God of Israel, Savior of all,” hear the angels speaking and announcing the good news to the shepherds: “Do not be afraid; we bring you good news of great joy: for today a Savior is born to you, who is Christ the Lord.” “For you are the God of Israel, Savior of all. Behold, all who oppose you will be put to shame and will go away in disgrace. They will be as though they did not exist, and will wear out like a garment.” By “those who oppose” he means those who resist the Word. For if you tell a pagan, or anyone else cut off from true religion, that there is a God, he does not fight you; but if you say that there is a Christ, he rages like one possessed. As the blessed David says somewhere: “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage. He is seated upon the cherubim; let the earth be shaken.” And who is the one seated there? Clearly the one to whom the same prophet says, “You who are seated upon the cherubim, shine forth; stir up your might, and come to save us.” You see that the mischief the heretics contrive finds no room in the wording. Rather, where there is equality of honor, he says, “I and the Father”; where there is the dispensation, he says, “He who sent me is greater than I”—greater because of the form of the sending, not because of the union of the divinity.

This, then, is how we must attend to the Scriptures, and not pass over the divine oracles. Now you condemn an entire Gospel, but the Savior does not condemn a single letter. He wanted us to be so reverent about Scripture that he said: “Truly, truly I tell you, it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota or one stroke of the law to fall.” So the Savior does not despise even the iota, but you tear apart a whole Scripture. And the passage clearly shows us that knowledge of the Scriptures is actually stronger than the resurrection of the dead. For the resurrection of the dead cannot do as much as the reading of the Scriptures. Listen to the patriarch Abraham, who hears the rich man say to him: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to tell my brothers not to come into this judgment.” And what does he say? “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.” But the rich man says, “No, father Abraham; unless someone rises from the dead, they will not believe.” And Abraham says to him: “Truly I tell you, if they will not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe even if someone rises from the dead.” Pay close attention. Would they, then, not have believed if someone had risen from the dead? Not at all. Consider the reasoning. Suppose someone appeared from the dead: it would be either one of the ancients, or one of our own time who was unknown, or one who was known. If it were one of the unknown, ignorance would have veiled the miracle. If Moses appeared today, how would you know that it was Moses? If Isaiah appeared today, how would you know that it was Isaiah? And if someone else who had died in our own time were raised, again the miracle would be overshadowed, some saying, “This is the man who died,” and others claiming, “This is not the one who died; it is some demon and phantom.” For unbelief is never at a loss for an evil road. And what wonder is it if human ingratitude could slander even a dead man who had risen? When the blind man was healed, “some said, ‘It is he’; others claimed, ‘No, but he is like him,’” while he himself said, “I am he.” He bore witness to himself, and the miracle cried out, yet ingratitude denied it. Did not many rise in the Savior’s time? “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep,” as Scripture says, after the dispensation of the cross, “rose from the tombs and went into the holy city and appeared to many.” Did the miracle quench unbelief, or conquer ingratitude? For signs are for unbelievers, not for believers; yet the unbeliever readily despises even signs. But see whether they showed respect for a dead man who had risen—how gladly they respected Lazarus! Lazarus rose from the dead, and since many were coming to see the Savior because of Lazarus’s resurrection, the Jews plotted to kill Lazarus. See how ingratitude never departs from its own character anywhere. With good reason, then, the patriarch said: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe him even if someone rises from the dead.” And so now too, the children of heretics, if they do not listen to Moses and the prophets and the Gospels, will not listen even if someone breaks forth with ten thousand voices. But let us not depart from the way. For “I am the way,” says the Lord. Whoever leaves the way, then, goes astray; whoever travels outside the Scriptures is caught in a storm. For just as at sea someone driven about by many winds cannot hold a straight course, but is tossed here and there by different winds, so too whoever gives himself over to various teachings and does not keep in step with the teaching of the gospel is no different from a merchant ship buffeted by the waves. That is why Scripture says, “Do not winnow with every wind,” and the interpreter adds, “and do not believe every word.” And so that you may learn that by “every wind” Scripture means every teaching, listen to Paul saying: “So that we may no longer be children, tossed by the waves and carried about by every wind of teaching, by human trickery, by craftiness in deceitful scheming.” “Every wind of teaching”: so “every wind” stands for “every teaching.” Whoever surrenders himself to it is tossed by the waves, caught in the storm, shipwrecked. For there is one voyage, one way, one harbor: faith. Faith guides, faith shelters, faith receives. But whoever falls away from faith is shipwrecked, as Paul says when writing to Timothy: “This charge I entrust to you, Timothy my child, that by it you may fight the good fight, holding faith and a good conscience; by rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith.” So whoever departs from the faith is shipwrecked, while whoever follows the faith brings his vessel to anchor in a calm harbor. Let us not, then, be carried off by every wind. After the Lord there is no other teaching. For after Moses, Christ was expected; but after Christ, no other is expected. That is why Moses, wishing to teach the people that they must not keep to his own laws alone but must await their fulfillment, said: “The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you; him you shall hear.” For if he had known his teaching to be complete, he would not have referred them to another teacher, saying: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me.” He says “a prophet” because he is from among you. As God he is not from among you, but as prophet he is from among you; for as God he is from God, but as prophet he is from among you according to the flesh. That is also why he says “like me”—that is, a lawgiver. For since Moses was the one ancient lawgiver, and the Savior the second lawgiver, not of one people but of the whole world, he therefore says “like me,” in type and in lawgiving. Who will bear witness to this statement? David, who lived a few generations after Moses, cried out: “Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you. Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them.” Now if David had lived before Moses, he might reasonably have been praying for Moses. But if Moses shone forth first, and David came later than Moses, why did the prophet David want to call for another lawgiver, when there already was one, saying, “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them”? Over whom, then, if not the nations? For he says, “Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you.” For the lawgiver has been given to the nations. “Let the nations know that they are men”; for before the lawgiver they were driven about like irrational beasts. But when God the Word comes, he restores them to their rational nature. So Moses, as I said before, declared, “The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you, like me”; David, “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them”; and Paul, who came after the Savior and was the Savior’s herald, seeing that those before had been to await Christ, but after Christ no one else, therefore says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.” He shuts out every other knowledge and takes the keys of the kingdom. And to show that after the teaching of Christ no other teaching is to be expected, he says: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.” And so as not to shut out human trickery alone, he presses the contest further and says: “Even if we.” Why on earth does he say “Even if we”? Could the Apostle have taught otherwise? Or is it clear that the divine Paul is using hyperbole: even if you hear me preaching other things, understand that I am not speaking from God? That is why he says “Even if we.” For a human tongue can be overturned, but the tongue of God does not change. Hence, “Even if we, even if an angel from heaven.” You might well have come to suspect that an angel from heaven was going to bring in a foreign teaching. But he is not guarding against angels; he is cutting off the trickery of the devil. “Even if an angel from heaven”—not because he knew such things of the angels, for he knew that among the angels the truth is free from error, but because Satan often transforms himself, and demons, often disguising themselves in the forms of angels, bring in teaching to suit their own notions, as it is said: “Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.” Therefore, on account of the disguise of the pretenders, he shuts out even the true angels, and pronounces his sentence against angels without qualification—not insulting them, but closing the road to the demons. And the angels were not indignant when Paul said, “Even if an angel from heaven preaches a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema”; rather, they rejoiced at the boldness of the preacher who was safeguarding and walling in the divine proclamation. That is why the angels themselves, having learned that one must believe nothing but the word of the apostles, are careful and do not preach. They are sent to human beings, but they certainly do not preach. An angel was once sent to Cornelius; he appears to him and announces his own ministry, saying, “Cornelius, your prayers and your alms have gone up as a memorial before God.” The announcing is mine, he is saying, but the preaching belongs to the apostles. For it belongs to an angel to know whether the manner of one’s service and prayer is acceptable; but the angel does not entrust the preaching to himself, but to the apostles. So he adds: “Send therefore to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter; he will come and speak words to you by which you and all your household will be saved.” And what prevented him from preaching on the spot? Would not the preaching of an angel have been more credible? Would not Cornelius have been more assured hearing about the cross, the passion and the dispensation from an angel? But the angel at once guards himself, not wishing to open up room for the demons, and at the same time shows us that there is no salvation outside the apostolic teaching. And if an angel from heaven who preaches something different is anathematized, will not the one who breathes the doctrines of Arius and teaches those of Eunomius and Sabellius rightly be anathematized, unless he first corrects himself through repentance? Consider, brothers, that these things are spoken not by us but by the holy martyr and through the intercessions of the Father. For these things are said in honor of the martyrs, since the honor of a martyr is the guarding of the faith. If, then, you too wish to honor the martyr, honor the one to whom the martyr bore witness. For if he shed his blood for Christ, will you not shed your blood for Christ? Having, then, this security of faith, let us strive to shine also with good works, so that having sown virtues we may reap rewards. For each person, from his own works, is a reaper of righteousness, as Paul says: “While we have time, let us do what is good. For in our proper season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary.” What proper season? That of the resurrection. So this present season is not our proper one, but another’s. Here are the seeds, there the sheaves; here you sow in affliction, there you reap in gladness, as David says: “Those who sow in tears will reap with rejoicing.” May it be granted to us both to sow and to reap with rejoicing, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
